blocks.text: **Chronic kidney disease (CKD)** is a loss of kidney function that has lasted **more than 3 months**, is usually **irreversible** and often creeps forward over years. Early on it is only an abnormal blood or urine result. Later, loss of the excretory, endocrine and metabolic roles of the kidney produces the multisystem syndrome called **uraemia**. **Stage 5**, where the patient is likely to die without renal replacement therapy (RRT), is called **end-stage renal disease (ESRD)**.

blocks.title: GFR (G) categories (eGFR in mL/min/1.73 m²)
rows: Anaemia in some; most progress slowly or not at all
First symptoms often below eGFR 20; electrolyte problems likely
Symptoms and complications usual; dialysis usually starts below 10

blocks.title: Albuminuria (A) categories: same cut-offs in different units
columns: Albumin excretion (mg/24 h or mg/g creatinine)

blocks.title: Rules for making and labelling the diagnosis
items: Use an **eGFR equation**, not creatinine alone, and get **two values about 3 months apart** before assigning a stage.
Stages G1 and G2 count as CKD **only with a marker of damage**: albuminuria or proteinuria, haematuria, abnormal imaging (e.g. structural abnormality), an inherited kidney disease or abnormal biopsy.
Report **both letters**, e.g. **G3bA3**. The A suffix is added because albuminuria strongly predicts outcome.

blocks.text: About **5–7%** of adults have CKD G3–G5 (eGFR < 60), mostly aged over 65. More than **a quarter of people over 75** have eGFR < 60, mostly G3a. In them it mainly signals **cardiovascular risk**, and very few ever reach ESRD. Most people with stage 1–3 disease do not lose function steadily and do not die of kidney failure.
Faced with a raised creatinine, the first question is **"what was it before?"** Previous results separate **AKI, CKD and acute-on-chronic** disease.
Classic trap: **eGFR 60–90 with A1 albuminuria and no other marker of damage is not CKD**. You need eGFR < 60 or evidence of kidney damage.

The albuminuria cut-offs look different between books (3 vs 30 for A1). They are the same categories in different units: UK texts use ACR in mg/mmol, US texts use mg/g or mg/24 h. Check the unit before you stage.

blocks.note: Look at: the classification grid that combines GFR (G) and albumin:creatinine ratio (A) categories.

blocks.title: Common causes of CKD (Davidson)
rows: Varies greatly by race and region
Causal role debated; may be secondary to another renal disease
Especially in older people with stage 3

blocks.title: Causes grouped by site
items: **Congenital / inherited**: polycystic kidney disease, tuberous sclerosis, cystinosis.
**Glomerular**: primary glomerulonephritis, diabetes, lupus, amyloid.
**Vascular**: hypertensive nephrosclerosis, renovascular disease, vasculitis.
**Tubulointerstitial**: drugs and analgesics (also NSAIDs, PPIs, lithium), reflux, TB, myeloma.
**Obstruction**: stones, prostatic disease, retroperitoneal fibrosis; schistosomiasis in parts of the Middle East.

blocks.text: **Diabetic kidney disease** is the commonest cause of ESRD in many countries: about **26% in the UK** and almost **half in the USA**. Diabetes, hypertension and atherosclerosis together account for over 70% of CKD. ESKD is 3–4 times commoner in people of black African descent, in whom hypertensive nephropathy is frequent.

blocks.title: The common pathway of progression
items: Loss of nephrons makes the **survivors hyperfilter and hypertrophy**.
Their **raised intraglomerular pressure** and shear stress injure them in turn. This shows as **new or rising proteinuria**.
**Angiotensin II** narrows the **efferent arteriole**, raising glomerular pressure further. It also drives **TGF-β** (pro-fibrotic) and **PAI-1** (blocks matrix breakdown).
Filtered protein is itself **toxic to proximal tubules**.
Whatever the first insult, the end result is **fibrosis** of glomeruli, tubules and small vessels.

blocks.text: Outlook is predicted by **hypertension** (especially when poorly controlled), **proteinuria** and the amount of **interstitial scarring** on biopsy, not by the glomerular lesion. Glomerular diseases tend to progress faster than tubulointerstitial ones.

blocks.title: Why the main complications happen
rows: Two drivers: **phosphate retention** and **failure of 1α-hydroxylation** of 25(OH)D. High phosphate raises **FGF23 and PTH**. Low calcitriol cuts gut calcium absorption, so calcium falls and PTH rises further (**secondary hyperparathyroidism**).
Long-standing stimulation makes the enlarged glands **autonomous**, giving **hypercalcaemia**.
Mainly **erythropoietin deficiency**, plus uraemic marrow suppression, shorter red cell survival, blood loss and poor iron intake/use.
Less renal mass makes less ammonia to buffer acid, and H⁺ excretion fails.

blocks.note: Look at: the flow from impaired renal function to high phosphate, low calcitriol, low calcium, high PTH and bone resorption, with FGF23 as a partial compensation.

blocks.text: CKD is usually picked up **incidentally** as a raised urea and creatinine on routine bloods, often while screening people with diabetes or hypertension. Most patients feel well until eGFR is **below about 30**. **Nocturia** (loss of concentrating ability) is an early but non-specific symptom.

blocks.title: As eGFR falls below 15–20
items: First: **tiredness and breathlessness** (anaemia, fluid overload).
Then: **pruritus, anorexia, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, hiccups**.
Very advanced: **Kussmaul breathing** (acidosis), muscle twitching, fits, drowsiness and coma.

blocks.title: Uraemia by system
rows: Sallow/yellow complexion, pallor, pruritus with scratch marks, easy bruising, brown-line nails, uraemic frost, **calciphylaxis**
Hypertension (CKD is the commonest cause of **secondary hypertension**), LVH, heart failure, **pericarditis**, accelerated atheroma
Encephalopathy, asterixis, myoclonus, seizures, symmetrical **peripheral neuropathy**, restless legs, **carpal tunnel** (β2-microglobulin amyloid)
Normocytic normochromic anaemia; bleeding from **platelet dysfunction**
Raised prolactin, low testosterone and erectile dysfunction, oligo-/amenorrhoea, poor growth in children; use **TSH** to judge thyroid status
Uraemic fetor and metallic taste, hypothermia, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis

blocks.title: Signs to look for at the bedside (OSCE)
items: Pallor, yellow tinge, excoriations, bruising, brown-line nail pigmentation.
Raised JVP and oedema (fluid overload); pericardial rub; pulsus paradoxus if tamponade.
Deep, fast breathing of acidosis.
Neuropathy: absent reflexes, reduced sensation, paraesthesia.
**Clues to RRT**: arteriovenous fistula, central dialysis line, **Tenckhoff catheter**, iliac-fossa transplant scar.

blocks.text: **Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death** in CKD, roughly **16 times** commoner than in the general population. Risk climbs as GFR falls and with proteinuria. **Sudden cardiac death** is especially common (LVH, vascular and valve calcification). **Infection** is the other major cause of death, as uraemia impairs cellular and humoral immunity. A successful transplant removes the excess cardiovascular risk of stage 5.

**Calciphylaxis** (calcific uraemic arteriolopathy): painful skin plaques that ulcerate into non-healing black eschars. Histology shows **calcification of small dermal vessels** with thrombosis and no vasculitis. Risks: hyperparathyroidism, high phosphate, obesity, diabetes, female sex and **warfarin**. Mortality is high, with many dying within a year.

**Uraemic pericarditis** (severe uraemia or under-dialysis) is often **haemorrhagic** and can cause tamponade and atrial arrhythmias, so be cautious with anticoagulation. It is an indication for (more intensive) dialysis.
Pruritus in CKD has several causes: retained waste, high calcium × phosphate product, hyperparathyroidism and iron deficiency. **Inadequate dialysis** is a treatable cause.

blocks.note: Look at: physical signs of advanced CKD, including the RRT clues (fistula, central line, Tenckhoff catheter, transplant scar).
Look at: body map of CKD symptoms and signs grouped by system.
Look at: calcified arterioles in the skin without vasculitis (calciphylaxis).

blocks.title: What the work-up is for
items: Exclude **AKI**: if urea and creatinine are unexpectedly high (a rise, or no old results), **repeat within 2 weeks**.
Find the **cause**, since it may change treatment.
Find **reversible factors** such as hypertension or obstruction.
Screen for **complications** (anaemia, bone disease) and **cardiovascular risk factors**.

blocks.title: Core tests in CKD
rows: Compare with previous results to judge stability
Haematuria + proteinuria suggests glomerular disease; proteinuria predicts progression and calls for ACEi/ARB
Exclude non-renal causes before calling it renal anaemia
Hepatitis B, C and HIV serology
Before dialysis or transplant; vaccinate against hepatitis B if not immune

blocks.title: Renal ultrasound
items: Indications: obstructive symptoms, persistent haematuria, family history of **polycystic kidney disease**, or **progressive / accelerated** CKD.
**Small kidneys** = chronic disease with little chance of recovery.
**Asymmetric** kidneys suggest renovascular or developmental disease.
Normal-sized or **large kidneys do not exclude CKD** (e.g. diabetes, polycystic disease).

blocks.text: Features that favour **chronic** over acute disease: **normochromic normocytic anaemia**, **small kidneys** and evidence of **renal osteodystrophy**. Renal anaemia can be severe (Hb 50–70 g/L in stage 5) but is often milder in polycystic kidney disease.

blocks.title: Reading the bone biochemistry and X-rays
rows: Subperiosteal erosions of fingers, **pepperpot skull**, osteitis fibrosa cystica
Autonomous glands after long-standing secondary disease
**Rugger-jersey spine**: dense end-plates with less dense centres
**Low PTH, normal ALP**, Ca may be high
Over-treatment with active vitamin D, after parathyroidectomy, aluminium binders, diabetes

blocks.title: Refer to a nephrologist if
items: Rapid decline: a fall of **> 25%**, or **> 15 mL/min/1.73 m² in a year**.
Heavy proteinuria: **ACR > 70** or PCR > 100 mg/mmol (unless known diabetic and already treated).
ACR > 30 mg/mmol **with** non-visible haematuria.
Hypertension uncontrolled on **4 or more** drugs.
Suspected renal involvement in a **multisystem disease**.

blocks.text: A renal **biopsy is rarely done** when both kidneys are small: it is riskier, less likely to give a diagnosis and seldom changes management.
Dipstick haematuria of 1+ or more is significant. It should also prompt a search for urinary tract malignancy (e.g. **bladder cancer**), not just kidney disease.

Urgent threats to check in any sick CKD patient: **hyperkalaemia** (get an ECG, but a normal ECG does not exclude it), **pulmonary oedema** (ask about recent weight gain) and **infection**. A **high FGF23** is the strongest independent predictor of death in CKD.

blocks.note: Look at: serial eGFR plotted over time; better BP control and less proteinuria flatten the slope and push back the date dialysis is needed (eGFR about 10).
Look at: CKD-MBD map linking each mechanism to its bone disease and X-ray sign.
Look at: renal osteodystrophy diagram (Looser zones, erosions, pepperpot skull, rugger-jersey spine, brown tumours).

sections.title: Conservative management: slowing progression and treating complications

blocks.title: Aims of care
items: Monitor function: every **6 months in stage 3**, more often in stages 4–5 or if falling fast. A plot of eGFR against time shows whether treatment works and predicts when RRT will be needed.
Slow progression: treat the cause, control **BP**, cut **proteinuria**, control diabetes.
Limit complications and treat **cardiovascular risk** (exercise, weight, stop smoking, statin).
Prepare for **RRT** in good time.

blocks.text: Books disagree on BP targets: NICE-based Zero to Finals uses < 140/90, or < 130/80 only if ACR > 70; Pocket Medicine and K&C Essentials aim for < 120/80. Follow **Davidson** (table above). All agree that any fall in BP helps.

blocks.title: ACE inhibitors and ARBs
items: Give to **all patients with diabetic nephropathy** and to CKD with proteinuria (**PCR > 50 or ACR > 30 mg/mmol**), **even if BP is normal**. They lower proteinuria, slow decline and reduce cardiovascular events and death.
Recheck U&E **7–10 days** after starting or increasing the dose. **Continue if eGFR falls ≤ 25%** and the fall is not progressive.
Do not start if **K⁺ > 5.5 mmol/L**. If K⁺ > 6.0, reduce or stop, but only after other potassium measures.
**Never combine ACEi + ARB** (or a direct renin inhibitor): no renal benefit, more hyperkalaemia and AKI.

blocks.text: K&C Essentials still suggests adding an ARB to a maximal ACE inhibitor for proteinuria > 1 g/day. **Davidson (and Pocket Medicine) say avoid dual blockade.** In an exam, dual ACEi + ARB is the wrong answer.

**SGLT2 inhibitors** cause a small early dip in eGFR, then cut the risk of CKD progression by about **30–40%** and lower mortality in proteinuric CKD, with or without diabetes (minimum eGFR about 25–30). Davidson notes the same benefit at the cost of more **genital infections**. Mineralocorticoid antagonists also slow progression in diabetic CKD.

blocks.title: "Sick-day rules": stop these during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever
items: ACE inhibitors (-pril) and ARBs (-sartan).
NSAIDs.
Diuretics.
Metformin.
Restart after **24–48 hours** of eating and drinking normally.

blocks.title: Treating the complications
rows: Sodium < 100 mmol/day, fluid restriction if severe, **loop diuretics** (escalating doses or combinations)

Potassium < 70 mmol/day (bananas, tomatoes, potatoes, chocolate, salt substitutes); **calcium resonium only short-term** (bowel necrosis); **patiromer / sodium zirconium cyclosilicate** for chronic use; treat acidosis
**Oral sodium bicarbonate** to keep plasma HCO₃⁻ **> 22 mmol/L** (Davidson starts at 1 g 8-hourly)
Low-phosphate diet; **binders with meals** (calcium carbonate, sevelamer, lanthanum, aluminium hydroxide); aim **PO4 ≤ 1.5 mmol/L**
**Alfacalcidol or calcitriol** if hypocalcaemic or PTH > 2× ULN; titrate PTH to **2–4× ULN** to avoid adynamic bone
**Parathyroidectomy**; cinacalcet (calcimimetic) if surgery fails or is not possible
Correct iron first (often IV), then an **ESA**; target **Hb 100–120 g/L**
Lifestyle, statin (e.g. atorvastatin 20 mg in NICE guidance); vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus

blocks.text: **ESAs** (epoetin, darbepoetin): correcting Hb to normal brings **hypertension and thrombosis** without a mortality gain, hence the 100–120 g/L target. About 30% develop hypertension. Poor response: look for **iron deficiency**, bleeding, infection/inflammation, malignancy (especially **myeloma**) and rarely anti-EPO antibodies (**pure red cell aplasia**). Avoid transfusion where possible: it **sensitises** against a future graft.

Numbers that differ between books (follow Davidson): **Hb target** 100–120 g/L (Pocket 10–11.5 g/dL, K&C Essentials 11–12 g/dL); **PTH target** 2–4× ULN (Kumar: 2–3× ULN once on dialysis); **protein intake**: avoid excess but **do not restrict severely**, as it causes malnutrition without slowing decline (Step-Up suggests 0.7–0.8 g/kg/day).

blocks.title: Drugs to avoid or adjust
items: **NSAIDs** and potassium-sparing diuretics or **potassium salt substitutes**.
**Opioids** accumulate and can cause narcosis; many drugs need dose adjustment.
**Gadolinium** contrast if eGFR < 30 or on dialysis: risk of **nephrogenic systemic fibrosis**.

blocks.text: In the **SHARP** trial, simvastatin plus ezetimibe prevented about a quarter of major atherosclerotic events in CKD, but did not improve survival or prevent ESKD. Lipid-lowering helps less once patients are on dialysis.

sections.title: Renal replacement therapy: when, which, or none

blocks.text: Start RRT when uraemic symptoms begin to **affect quality of life** but **before serious complications**, typically as eGFR approaches **10 mL/min/1.73 m²**. Starting earlier brings no benefit. Preparation should begin **at least 12 months** ahead: choice of modality, **access** (fistula or PD catheter), **hepatitis B vaccination** and psychological and social support. Late referral is linked to worse outcomes.

blocks.title: Indications for dialysis
rows: Oedema or pulmonary oedema despite diuretics; severe hypertension
K⁺ generally > 6.5 mmol/L with ECG changes
K⁺ resistant to diet and drugs
Anorexia, nausea, lethargy; usually only when eGFR < 10
Anaemia despite EPO and iron; phosphate despite binders

blocks.text: Mnemonic for acute indications, **AEIOU**: **A**cidosis, **E**lectrolytes (resistant K⁺), **I**ntoxication with a dialysable drug (methanol, ethylene glycol, lithium, aspirin), **O**edema (refractory pulmonary), **U**raemia (pericarditis, encephalopathy, seizures).
A creatinine or urea **number alone is not an indication** for dialysis. The decision is clinical; uraemic pericarditis and encephalopathy are absolute indications.

blocks.title: Haemodialysis vs peritoneal dialysis
rows: Efficient; about 4 h three times a week
Less efficient; CAPD four exchanges a day, or APD overnight for 8–10 h
An **intact peritoneal cavity** without major surgical scarring

blocks.title: Haemodialysis: key numbers
items: Blood is pumped through a dialyser; solutes diffuse across a semipermeable membrane down a concentration gradient. Blood flow at least 200 mL/min, with **heparin** anticoagulation.
Usually **3–5 hours, three times a week** (Davidson; Kumar and K&C Essentials say 4–5 h).
Adequacy: **urea reduction ratio > 65%**; below this, mortality rises.
More dialysis (extra sessions, short daily, or nocturnal) improves fluid and phosphate control.

blocks.title: Peritoneal dialysis: key facts
items: A permanent catheter (**Tenckhoff**) sits in the peritoneal cavity.
**CAPD**: about **2 L** of glucose-containing fluid is left for 4–6 h, four times a day. The hyperosmolar fluid draws water out (ultrafiltration).
**APD**: a machine does the exchanges overnight.
Suits children, adults with **residual renal function** and older people with cardiovascular instability.

blocks.text: **Conservative (non-dialytic) care** of stage 5 CKD is a positive choice for **older patients with many comorbidities**. Survival may be similar or only slightly shorter, without the admissions and procedures of dialysis. It includes treating anaemia and other complications and **palliative care** at the end. Stopping dialysis is appropriate when quality of life falls irreversibly.
UK picture (Davidson): of patients on RRT, about **53% have a working transplant**, 41% are on HD and 6% on PD. Transplantation is the **only cure**.

blocks.note: Look at: the four RRT options: haemodialysis, haemofiltration, peritoneal dialysis and a transplant joined to the external iliac vessels.
Look at: diffusion across the dialyser: K⁺, urea and water leave the blood; bicarbonate enters it.

blocks.title: Haemodialysis access options
rows: Arterialises in about **4–6 weeks** (Davidson); create up to a year before dialysis
Needs good arm vessels; thrombosis, aneurysm, steal
More infection and thrombosis than a fistula
**Highest bloodstream infection risk**, thrombosis, malfunction, **central venous stenosis**

blocks.text: **Protect the veins.** In anyone with progressive CKD, do not put cannulas, take blood or measure BP in the arm needed for a future fistula (usually the **non-dominant** forearm for a radiocephalic fistula). For temporary access use the **internal jugular or femoral** vein and **avoid subclavian lines**: they bleed, and stenosis there can ruin a fistula in that arm.

Fistula maturation times differ: Davidson 4–6 weeks; Zero to Finals 4 weeks to 4 months; Pocket Medicine 2–6 months. Follow Davidson. Kumar adds that the fistula is made when creatinine is about **400–500 µmol/L**, and earlier in diabetics.

blocks.title: Examining an AV fistula (OSCE)
items: Look: skin integrity, scars, **aneurysms**, signs of infection.
Feel: a continuous **thrill** over the anastomosis.
Listen: a **"machinery" bruit**.
**No thrill and no bruit = thrombosed fistula.**
Never take blood from or cannulate the fistula for routine bloods.

blocks.title: Fistula complications
items: Thrombosis and stenosis.
Aneurysm and infection.
**Steal syndrome**: distal hand ischaemia because blood is diverted through the fistula.
**High-output heart failure** from the extra preload.

blocks.text: **Line-related sepsis.** Bloodstream infection between or during sessions presents with **rigors, fever and hypotension**, and the source is usually the **access** (especially a catheter, which leaves a foreign body in the circulation). Take **blood cultures**, start empirical **vancomycin plus Gram-negative cover** (Gram-positive cocci, notably _S. aureus_, are commonest), then remove or exchange the catheter depending on the organism; antibiotic **"locks"** are an option. Seeding causes **endocarditis**, septic arthritis and **vertebral infection**. Sepsis is, after cardiovascular disease, a leading cause of death on dialysis.

blocks.title: Problems during or between haemodialysis sessions
rows: Sudden fall in BP, leg cramps, sometimes chest pain
K⁺ and acid–base shifts; check K⁺ and gases
Heparin, needle disconnection; consider heparin-free dialysis
Faulty or disconnected lines; stop dialysis
Collapse, chest or back pain soon after starting
Reaction to membrane or sterilant; change dialyser
Headache, vomiting, confusion, **fits** in the first sessions
Cerebral oedema from rapid urea removal; start with **short 1–2 h sessions**

blocks.title: Peritoneal dialysis complications
rows: **Cloudy effluent** (> 100 white cells/mm³, mostly neutrophils), abdominal pain; about 1 episode per 2 patient-years
Culture fluid; **intraperitoneal** antibiotics (e.g. vancomycin, tobramycin); remove catheter for fungi or _Pseudomonas_ or if refractory
_S. epidermidis_ 40–50%, Gram-negatives ~25%, _S. aureus_ ~15%; TB and fungi rare
Usually skin contaminants entering via the catheter
Redness and pus at exit site
Fluid overload as glucose is absorbed and the gradient lost
Recurrent small-bowel obstruction, malnutrition, after many years
Hernias, weight gain/hyperglycaemia, protein loss, right pleural effusion

blocks.note: Look at: the three HD access types: tunnelled catheter into the right atrium, AV fistula with a distended vein, and AV graft.
Look at: an IV cannula sited in the non-dominant forearm of a CKD patient, exactly where a future fistula is needed.
Look at: a radiocephalic fistula in the left forearm, with a warning not to compress it during surgery.
Look at: the course of a Tenckhoff PD catheter with its tip in the pelvis.

blocks.text: Transplantation gives the **best long-term survival** in ESRD and is the **most cost-effective** RRT. Everyone with ESRD should be considered; there is **no absolute age limit**. Common contraindications: **active malignancy**, active vasculitis, significant **cardiovascular disease**, active infection, non-adherence or substance misuse, and a high risk of disease recurrence. **Living-donor** and **pre-emptive** (before dialysis) transplants do best. Benefits include freedom from dialysis diet and fluid limits, correction of anaemia and infertility, and less need for parathyroidectomy.

blocks.title: Matching and surgery
items: **ABO compatibility** is usually required.
HLA matching (especially **HLA-DR**) reduces rejection; HLA genes sit on chromosome 6.
A positive **cross-match** for anti-HLA antibodies predicts early rejection. Incompatible living-donor transplants are possible after desensitisation, and paired exchange schemes help.

Graft goes in the **iliac fossa** (pelvis): donor artery and vein to the **external iliac** vessels, donor ureter to the **bladder**. Native kidneys usually stay (removed only for recurrent sepsis or huge polycystic kidneys). Look for a **"hockey-stick" scar** and a palpable graft.

blocks.title: Immunosuppressants
rows: **Impaired wound healing**, so not used early

blocks.title: Graft dysfunction by time after transplant
rows: Renal artery/vein **thrombosis**, ureteric leak, **delayed graft function** (ATN), **hyperacute rejection** (pre-formed anti-HLA antibodies)
**Acute rejection**, especially in the first 3 months

blocks.text: **Delayed graft function** from ATN is the commonest early problem in deceased-donor grafts (up to **40–50%**). Risks: donation after circulatory death, long **cold ischaemia time**, high tacrolimus level. Do not call it rejection: acute rejection (10–30%) usually shows up within the first 3 months, and needs biopsy.

blocks.title: Treating rejection
items: **Acute cellular rejection**: IV **methylprednisolone** on 3 consecutive days; **ATG** if steroid-resistant.
**Antibody-mediated rejection**: donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies plus **C4d** staining on biopsy. Treat with **plasma exchange, IVIG** and anti-CD20 (rituximab).
Late dysfunction work-up: drug levels, donor-specific antibodies, BK viral load, ultrasound, then biopsy.

blocks.title: Infection and late complications
items: Early: ordinary **bacterial** infections (urine, wound, chest).
**CMV**, especially a seronegative recipient of a seropositive kidney: prevent with **valganciclovir**.
**Pneumocystis**: prevent with **co-trimoxazole**.
**BK polyomavirus** nephropathy: **reduce immunosuppression**.
Malignancy: **skin cancer** (especially **SCC**; about half of white recipients by 15 years), **EBV-related PTLD** / non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
**Cardiovascular disease** causes about half of deaths; steroid diabetes and osteoporosis.
Recurrence: **FSGS** (often early) and MCGN; later IgA and membranous nephropathy.

blocks.text: Transplant adds roughly **10 years of life** compared with staying on dialysis, and it reverses the excess cardiovascular risk of stage 5.

blocks.note: Look at: (A) acute vascular rejection with endothelialitis; (B) antibody-mediated rejection with glomerulitis and peritubular capillary C4d staining.

cards.front: What do you need before assigning a CKD stage?
cards.back: Two eGFR values about **3 months apart** (CKD = abnormality lasting > 3 months).

cards.front: eGFR range of CKD G3a and G3b?
Albuminuria categories in UK units (ACR, mg/mmol)?
Is eGFR 75 with ACR 1 mg/mmol and normal urine and imaging CKD?
cards.back: **No.** G1–G2 needs a marker of kidney damage to count as CKD.

cards.front: Commonest cause of ESRD in many countries?
cards.back: **Diabetic kidney disease** (about 26% in the UK, nearly 50% in the USA).

cards.front: How does angiotensin II drive CKD progression?
cards.back: Constricts the **efferent arteriole** (↑ glomerular pressure) and upregulates **TGF-β** and **PAI-1**, promoting fibrosis.

cards.front: The two primary drivers of renal bone disease?
cards.back: **Phosphate retention** and failure to convert 25(OH)D to **1,25(OH)₂D**.

cards.front: Below what eGFR do most CKD patients first get symptoms?
cards.back: Usually below **30**; symptoms common below **15–20**. Nocturia is an early non-specific symptom.

cards.front: Risk factors for calciphylaxis?
cards.back: Hyperparathyroidism, high phosphate, obesity, diabetes, female sex and **warfarin**.

cards.front: Leading cause of death in CKD?
cards.back: **Cardiovascular disease** (about 16-fold excess), especially sudden cardiac death.

cards.front: Unexpectedly high creatinine with no old results: next step?
cards.back: **Repeat renal function within 2 weeks** so AKI is not missed.

cards.front: Indications for renal ultrasound in CKD?
cards.back: Obstructive symptoms, persistent haematuria, family history of **PKD**, or **progressive** CKD.

cards.front: What is a "rugger-jersey spine"?
cards.back: Bands of sclerotic end-plates and less dense vertebral centres: **osteosclerosis** from long-standing hyperparathyroidism in CKD.

cards.front: Rapid-decline criterion for nephrology referral?
cards.back: eGFR fall **> 25%** or **> 15 mL/min/1.73 m² per year**.

cards.front: After starting an ACEi in CKD: when to recheck and what fall is acceptable?
cards.back: Recheck at **7–10 days**; continue if eGFR falls **≤ 25%** and is not progressive.

cards.front: Which drugs go on a CKD sick-day card?
cards.back: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs, diuretics and metformin.

cards.front: Target Hb on ESA therapy (Davidson)?
cards.back: **100–120 g/L**. Normalising Hb raises hypertension and thrombosis with no survival gain.

cards.front: Targets for bicarbonate and phosphate in CKD?
cards.back: Bicarbonate **> 22 mmol/L**; phosphate **≤ 1.5 mmol/L**.

cards.front: When is RRT usually started in CKD?
cards.back: When symptoms impair quality of life, before serious complications; typically **eGFR about 10**. Early start gives no benefit.

cards.front: Haemodialysis adequacy target?
cards.back: **Urea reduction ratio > 65%**.

cards.front: Why avoid subclavian lines in kidney patients?
cards.back: Bleeding risk, and **subclavian stenosis/thrombosis** can wreck a future arm fistula.

cards.front: Commonest organism in PD peritonitis?
cards.back: _Staphylococcus epidermidis_ (40–50%).

cards.front: How do you know an AV fistula is patent?
cards.back: Palpable **thrill** and audible **machinery bruit**; their absence suggests thrombosis.

cards.front: Where is a kidney transplant placed?
cards.back: In the **iliac fossa**: vessels to the **external iliac** artery and vein, ureter to the bladder; native kidneys usually left.

cards.front: Standard maintenance immunosuppression after kidney transplant?
cards.back: **Tacrolimus (or ciclosporin) + mycophenolate (or azathioprine) + prednisolone**.

cards.front: Dangerous interaction for a transplant patient on azathioprine?
cards.back: **Allopurinol** (marrow toxicity).

questions.stem: A man aged 58 who has type 2 diabetes has an eGFR of 52 mL/min/1.73 m² and, three months later, 49 mL/min/1.73 m². His urine albumin:creatinine ratio is 45 mg/mmol on two samples.
questions.leadIn: How should his chronic kidney disease be classified?
questions.explanation: Both eGFR values (3 months apart) sit in **45–59 = G3a**. An ACR **above 30 mg/mmol = A3**. So the label is **G3aA3**.
whyNot: G2 needs eGFR 60–89.
A2 is ACR 3–30 mg/mmol; his is 45.
G3b is eGFR 30–44.
G4 is eGFR 15–29.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman has a routine eGFR of 84 mL/min/1.73 m², repeated at 3 months as 86. Urine ACR is 1.2 mg/mmol, dipstick shows no blood and a renal ultrasound is normal. She has no family history of kidney disease.
questions.leadIn: Which is the correct classification?
questions.explanation: An eGFR of 60–89 only counts as CKD when there is a **marker of kidney damage** (albuminuria, haematuria, structural or inherited disease, biopsy change). She has none, so she **does not have CKD**.
whyNot: G2 requires evidence of kidney damage, which she lacks.
G1 is eGFR > 90 and also needs evidence of damage.
A2 needs ACR 3–30 mg/mmol; hers is 1.2.
G3a needs eGFR 45–59.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man lost about half his nephrons to reflux nephropathy in childhood. The original cause has long been inactive, yet over 10 years his eGFR keeps falling and new proteinuria has appeared.
questions.leadIn: Which process best explains his continuing decline?
options: Afferent arteriolar constriction lowering glomerular pressure
Hyperfiltration and raised glomerular pressure in surviving nephrons
Suppression of TGF-β in the interstitium
questions.explanation: After nephron loss, the **remaining nephrons hyperfilter and hypertrophy**. Raised intraglomerular pressure (worsened by angiotensin II on the efferent arteriole) damages them, shown by **new or rising proteinuria**, and leads to fibrosis whatever the first insult was.
whyNot: Angiotensin II constricts the efferent, not afferent, arteriole and pressure rises, not falls.
CKD causes erythropoietin deficiency, not excess.
TGF-β is upregulated and drives fibrosis.
Hypercalcaemia does not explain progressive proteinuria and decline.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with CKD G4 has calcium 2.02 mmol/L, phosphate 1.9 mmol/L and a PTH four times the upper limit of normal.
questions.leadIn: Which change most directly reduces her intestinal calcium absorption?
questions.explanation: The failing tubules cannot **1α-hydroxylate 25(OH)D**, so calcitriol is low and **gut calcium absorption falls**. Together with phosphate binding calcium, this causes hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
whyNot: FGF23 is a response to high phosphate and mainly increases phosphate excretion; low calcitriol is the direct cause of poor gut uptake.
PTH is a consequence of low calcium, and it raises rather than lowers calcium.
Acidosis worsens bone disease but is not the main cause of low gut calcium uptake.
Not a recognised driver of reduced calcium absorption here.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with CKD G5 who has refused dialysis planning has 4 days of sharp central chest pain, worse lying flat. His JVP is raised, there is a scratchy sound at the left sternal edge and the ECG shows widespread changes with atrial fibrillation. Urea is 48 mmol/L.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Positional chest pain with a **friction rub** in severe **untreated uraemia** points to **uraemic pericarditis**. It is often haemorrhagic, can cause tamponade (raised JVP) and atrial arrhythmias, and is an indication for dialysis.
whyNot: MI pain is not positional and a rub would be unusual at onset.
PE does not cause a pericardial rub.
Dissection gives tearing pain radiating to the back and pulse deficits.
Would not explain the rub, raised JVP or arrhythmia.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old obese woman with diabetes has been on haemodialysis for 5 years and takes long-term warfarin for atrial fibrillation. Her PTH and phosphate are persistently high. She now has exquisitely painful purple plaques on both thighs, some with black, non-healing centres.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: **Calciphylaxis** (calcific uraemic arteriolopathy): painful plaques that ulcerate to eschar, from **calcification of small skin vessels** with thrombosis. Her risk factors are dialysis, hyperparathyroidism, high phosphate, obesity, diabetes, female sex and warfarin.
whyNot: NSF follows gadolinium and gives thickened, tethered skin, not necrotic eschars.
Cellulitis is a spreading erythema with fever, not bilateral necrotic plaques in this setting.
No associated inflammatory disease is described, and her dialysis-related risk factors point to calciphylaxis.
Histology of calciphylaxis shows calcification without vasculitis.

questions.stem: Blood tests at his new GP practice show a creatinine of 210 µmol/L in a 70-year-old man. He feels well and there are no previous results available.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Diagnose CKD G3b and repeat in 6 months
questions.explanation: With an unexpectedly high creatinine and **no baseline**, AKI must be excluded: **repeat within 2 weeks**. CKD can only be diagnosed when abnormality persists over 3 months.
whyNot: A single value cannot establish CKD, and AKI could be missed.
Biopsy is not a first step and is rarely done when kidneys are small.
There is no indication for RRT planning yet.
Iodinated contrast in possible AKI adds risk without first answering the key question.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old diabetic woman on haemodialysis has taken high-dose alfacalcidol and a calcium-based binder for years. Bloods: calcium 2.74 mmol/L (high), phosphate 1.4 mmol/L, alkaline phosphatase normal and PTH below the target range. DXA shows osteopenia.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely bone disorder?
questions.explanation: **Low PTH, normal ALP and high calcium** after over-treatment with active vitamin D (diabetes also raises risk) = **adynamic bone disease**: low turnover, so excess calcium cannot be laid down in bone.
whyNot: Secondary hyperparathyroidism has low calcium and high PTH and ALP.
Tertiary disease has hypercalcaemia but with a very high PTH.
Osteomalacia has low calcium and Looser zones, not low PTH with hypercalcaemia.
This is the high-turnover lesion of hyperparathyroidism, with high PTH.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man with CKD G3b and ACR 60 mg/mmol starts ramipril. Ten days later his creatinine has risen from 180 to 205 µmol/L (eGFR down about 15%) and potassium is 5.1 mmol/L. He feels well.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate action?
options: Continue ramipril and recheck renal function
Add losartan to increase antiproteinuric effect
questions.explanation: A small early fall in eGFR is expected as glomerular pressure drops. **Continue** if the fall is **≤ 25%** and not progressive, and K⁺ is acceptable. Recheck to make sure it stabilises.
whyNot: Stopping would lose the renal and cardiovascular benefit; the fall is within the accepted limit.
Dual ACEi + ARB gives no renal benefit and more hyperkalaemia and AKI.
A direct renin inhibitor is also not a useful addition or swap here and is avoided in combination.
Calcium resonium is only for very short-term use (bowel necrosis); his K⁺ does not need it.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman with CKD G4 is tired. Hb is 88 g/L, normocytic. Ferritin is 60 µg/L and transferrin saturation 14%. B12 and folate are normal and there is no bleeding.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate first treatment for her anaemia?
options: Intravenous iron, then review for an ESA
Start epoetin now with a target Hb of 140 g/L
questions.explanation: She is **iron deficient**. Correct iron first (often **IV**), then start an **ESA** if still anaemic. ESAs work poorly in iron deficiency, and the Hb target is **100–120 g/L**.
whyNot: Normalising Hb increases hypertension and thrombosis without lowering mortality; iron first.
Transfusion sensitises against a future graft and is not first-line.
Folate levels are normal.
ESAs work poorly in iron deficiency.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with CKD G5 (eGFR 8) awaiting a fistula becomes drowsy and confused over 2 days. He has a flapping tremor. Potassium is 5.6 mmol/L, bicarbonate 17 mmol/L and creatinine 780 µmol/L.
questions.leadIn: Which finding is the clearest indication to start dialysis now?
questions.explanation: Confusion with asterixis in advanced CKD is **uraemic encephalopathy**, an **absolute** indication for dialysis. The decision is clinical, not driven by a creatinine number.
whyNot: A creatinine value alone is never an indication.
K⁺ 5.6 can be managed medically; dialysis is for K⁺ resistant to treatment or > 6.5 with ECG changes.
Mild acidosis is treated with oral bicarbonate; severe means pH < 7.1.
A low eGFR alone, without symptoms or complications, does not mandate dialysis.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with CKD G5 wants to dialyse at home and keep working. He has had three laparotomies for adhesional bowel obstruction.
questions.leadIn: Which feature makes peritoneal dialysis least suitable for him?
options: Extensive peritoneal scarring from previous surgery
questions.explanation: PD needs an **intact peritoneal cavity**. Major scarring from previous abdominal surgery prevents effective exchanges. The other features actually favour PD.
whyNot: PD at home suits people who want to work.
Residual renal function favours PD as a first treatment.
PD is done at home, which suits him.
Age is not a contraindication to PD.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman dialyses through a tunnelled right internal jugular catheter while her fistula matures. One hour into a session she develops rigors, temperature 39.2 °C and BP 86/50 mmHg. The exit site looks normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Blood cultures, then IV vancomycin plus Gram-negative cover
Oral amoxicillin and continue the session
Paracetamol and review at the next session
questions.explanation: Rigors, fever and hypotension on HD point to **access-related bloodstream infection**. Take **blood cultures** and give empirical **vancomycin with Gram-negative cover** (Gram-positive cocci are commonest); then remove or exchange the catheter according to the organism.
whyNot: Oral narrow-spectrum treatment is inadequate for septic shock and misses staphylococci.
Intraperitoneal antibiotics treat PD peritonitis, not line sepsis.
The infected device is the catheter, not the immature fistula.
This is sepsis and needs immediate treatment.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man on CAPD notices that his drained fluid is cloudy and he has mild abdominal pain. The effluent white cell count is 420/mm³, 85% neutrophils.
questions.leadIn: Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: **PD peritonitis** (cloudy effluent, > 100 cells/mm³) is usually caused by **skin contaminants** entering via the catheter, most often _S. epidermidis_ (40–50%).
whyNot: Gram-negatives cause about a quarter; bowel organisms are less common.
An uncommon cause; it often needs catheter removal.
Fungi cause only about 2%.
TB causes only about 2% of CAPD peritonitis.

questions.stem: Six weeks after a deceased-donor kidney transplant, a 39-year-old woman’s creatinine rises from 120 to 190 µmol/L. Her tacrolimus level is in range, ultrasound shows good perfusion and no obstruction, and biopsy shows tubulitis and endothelialitis with negative C4d.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate first treatment?
questions.explanation: Weeks after transplant, with C4d-negative cellular infiltrates, this is **acute cellular rejection**. First-line treatment is **pulsed IV methylprednisolone for 3 days**, with ATG if steroid-resistant.
whyNot: Reducing immunosuppression suits CNI toxicity or BK virus, not rejection; levels are in range.
This is for antibody-mediated rejection (C4d positive, donor-specific antibodies).
Treats CMV, which the biopsy does not suggest.
Irrelevant here, and dangerous with azathioprine.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old kidney transplant recipient on prednisolone, ciclosporin and azathioprine is started on a new drug for recurrent gout. Three weeks later he has mouth ulcers and his FBC shows pancytopenia.
questions.leadIn: Which drug was most likely added?
questions.explanation: **Allopurinol** blocks xanthine oxidase, which breaks down azathioprine. Azathioprine levels rise and cause **marrow suppression**. This interaction is classic in transplant patients.
whyNot: Colchicine does not interact with azathioprine in this way.
Paracetamol does not cause this interaction.
Opioids accumulate in renal impairment and cause narcosis, not marrow suppression.
Topical NSAIDs have minimal systemic effect and do not raise azathioprine levels.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely answer from the list. Any option can be picked once, several times or not at all.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman with hypertension has eGFR values of 40 and 38 mL/min/1.73 m², 3 months apart. Urine ACR is 45 mg/mmol on repeat.
items.explanation: Step 1: confirm chronicity (two values 3 months apart). Step 2: eGFR 30–44 = **G3b**. Step 3: ACR > 30 mg/mmol = **A3**. Answer **G3bA3**.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man with type 1 diabetes has eGFR 75 mL/min/1.73 m² on two occasions and a persistent ACR of 12 mg/mmol.
items.explanation: Step 1: eGFR 75 alone would not be CKD. Step 2: ACR 3–30 is **A2 albuminuria**, a marker of kidney damage, so it is CKD. Step 3: eGFR 60–89 = **G2**. Answer **G2A2**.

items.stem: A 29-year-old athlete has eGFR 82 mL/min/1.73 m² on two tests. ACR is 1 mg/mmol, dipstick is clear and an ultrasound is normal.
items.explanation: Step 1: eGFR is ≥ 60. Step 2: look for any marker of damage: none (A1, no haematuria, normal imaging). Step 3: G1/G2 with A1 and no damage is **not CKD**.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man receives a kidney from a donor after circulatory death, with a cold ischaemia time of 22 hours. On day 2 his urine output is minimal and he needs dialysis. Ultrasound shows a well-perfused graft with no hydronephrosis or collection, and his tacrolimus level is in range.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of graft dysfunction?
options: Delayed graft function due to acute tubular necrosis
questions.explanation: Step 1, **timing**: day 2 points to the "hours to days" group (vessel thrombosis, ureteric leak, delayed graft function, hyperacute rejection). Step 2, **ultrasound**: good perfusion rules out vessel thrombosis, and no collection or hydronephrosis makes a leak or obstruction unlikely. Step 3, **risk factors**: DCD donor and long cold ischaemia are classic for **delayed graft function from ATN**, which affects up to 40–50% of deceased-donor grafts. Hyperacute rejection is caused by pre-formed anti-HLA antibodies, which the pre-transplant cross-match is designed to detect, and nothing here points to it over the classic DGF risk factors.
whyNot: Hyperacute rejection is due to pre-formed anti-HLA antibodies picked up by the pre-transplant cross-match; the DCD donor and long cold ischaemia point to DGF instead.
Acute rejection usually appears after the first days, mostly within 3 months.
BK nephropathy appears months after transplant.
Chronic injury develops over years.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely answer from the list. Any option can be picked once, several times or not at all.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man who has been on haemodialysis for 14 years wakes at night with numbness in both hands. Tinel’s sign is positive bilaterally and he has aching shoulders.
items.explanation: Long-term dialysis plus **bilateral carpal tunnel** and arthropathy = **β2-microglobulin amyloid**.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman with CKD G4 has calcium 1.98 mmol/L, phosphate 2.0 mmol/L, raised ALP and PTH four times the upper limit. Hand X-rays show erosions along the radial sides of the middle phalanges.
items.explanation: Low calcium, high phosphate, high ALP and high PTH with **subperiosteal erosions** = **secondary hyperparathyroidism**.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man had years of poorly controlled PTH on dialysis. Alfacalcidol was stopped 3 months ago, yet his calcium remains 2.85 mmol/L and his PTH is still very high.
items.explanation: Two steps: hypercalcaemia persists **after** stopping vitamin D, so it is not iatrogenic; with a **very high PTH** the glands have become **autonomous** = **tertiary hyperparathyroidism** (treated by parathyroidectomy).

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman on haemodialysis had an MRI with contrast for back pain. Two months later the skin of her legs has become thickened, tight and tethered, limiting movement.
items.explanation: **Gadolinium** in a patient with eGFR < 30 or on dialysis → **nephrogenic systemic fibrosis**.

questions.theme: Next step in the assessment of reduced kidney function
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most appropriate next step from the list. Any option can be picked once, several times or not at all.
options: Repeat eGFR in 3 months before staging
Hepatitis B, C and HIV serology

items.stem: A 42-year-old man with hypertension has eGFR 56 mL/min/1.73 m². His father and an aunt both needed dialysis for "cysts on the kidneys".
items.explanation: A **family history of polycystic kidney disease** is an indication for **renal ultrasound**.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman with CKD has had eGFR measurements of 48 and then 31 mL/min/1.73 m² twelve months apart. Her BP is controlled on two drugs.
items.explanation: Two steps: the fall is 17 mL/min in a year (> 15) and about 35% (> 25%), which is **rapid decline**, so **refer to nephrology**.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man with CKD G4 on ramipril and spironolactone feels weak. Potassium is 6.8 mmol/L on a non-haemolysed sample.
items.explanation: Severe hyperkalaemia: get an **ECG** immediately to look for changes that need emergency treatment (bearing in mind a normal ECG does not exclude danger).

items.stem: A 66-year-old smoker has eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73 m², ACR < 3 mg/mmol and 2+ blood on dipstick on two occasions. Urine culture is negative.
items.explanation: Significant haematuria **without proteinuria** in an older smoker needs a **malignancy work-up** of the urinary tract (e.g. bladder cancer).

questions.theme: Managing complications of chronic kidney disease
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most appropriate treatment from the list. Any option can be picked once, several times or not at all.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man with CKD G4 is well. Venous bicarbonate is 16 mmol/L on two occasions; potassium is 4.9 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Chronic acidosis worsens catabolism and bone disease and may speed decline: give **oral sodium bicarbonate** to keep HCO₃⁻ > 22 mmol/L.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman with CKD G4 has Hb 91 g/L. Ferritin is 420 µg/L, transferrin saturation 31%, B12 and folate are normal and there is no bleeding.
items.explanation: Two steps: iron stores are **replete** and other causes excluded, so this is renal anaemia from EPO deficiency: start an **ESA**, aiming for Hb 100–120 g/L.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man with CKD G3b takes lisinopril, furosemide and metformin. He has had diarrhoea and vomiting for 2 days and is struggling to drink.
items.explanation: Sick-day rules: **temporarily stop** ACEi/ARB (and diuretics, metformin, NSAIDs) until eating and drinking normally for 24–48 h.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman on haemodialysis has a phosphate of 2.3 mmol/L on repeated checks despite seeing the dietitian. Calcium is normal and PTH is within target.
items.explanation: Persistent **hyperphosphataemia** despite diet needs a **phosphate binder** taken with food, aiming for phosphate ≤ 1.5 mmol/L.

questions.theme: Complications of dialysis access and treatment
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely answer from the list. Any option can be picked once, several times or not at all.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man with a left radiocephalic fistula had a long episode of low blood pressure during yesterday’s dialysis. This morning there is no thrill over the fistula and no bruit.
items.explanation: Loss of **thrill and bruit**, especially after hypotension, = **fistula thrombosis**.

items.stem: A 64-year-old diabetic woman has a new left brachiocephalic fistula. During each session her left fingers become cold, pale and painful.
items.explanation: Distal hand ischaemia because blood is diverted through the fistula = **steal syndrome**.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man with severe AKI and a urea of 62 mmol/L has his first haemodialysis, a 4-hour session. Near the end he develops headache, vomiting and then a seizure.
items.explanation: Too rapid urea removal causes **cerebral oedema** = **disequilibrium syndrome**. First sessions should be short (1–2 h).

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman had several temporary subclavian dialysis lines before a fistula was formed in the same arm. Her whole arm is now swollen with distended veins over the shoulder and chest wall.
items.explanation: Previous subclavian/central catheters → **central venous stenosis**, which obstructs outflow from a fistula in that arm.

items.stem: A 49-year-old man stopped peritoneal dialysis after 9 years. He now has weight loss and repeated episodes of vomiting, colicky pain and distension due to small-bowel obstruction.
items.explanation: Long-term PD with **recurrent small-bowel obstruction** and malnutrition = **encapsulating (sclerosing) peritonitis**.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely answer from the list. Any option can be picked once, several times or not at all.

items.stem: Five months after a kidney transplant on intensive immunosuppression, with a ureteric stent left in for 6 weeks, a 45-year-old man’s creatinine is creeping up. Tacrolimus level is in range and a plasma viral PCR shows a high polyomavirus load.
items.explanation: Months after transplant, intensive immunosuppression, ureteric stent and high polyomavirus load = **BK nephropathy**: reduce immunosuppression.

items.stem: A CMV-seronegative woman received a kidney from a seropositive donor. Her prophylaxis was stopped early. Seven weeks later she has fever and malaise, and a viral PCR on blood is positive.
items.explanation: Two steps: **D+/R−** mismatch is the highest-risk group, and missed **valganciclovir** prophylaxis leaves her exposed = **CMV** infection.

items.stem: A 33-year-old whose own kidneys failed from primary FSGS has heavy proteinuria within 3 weeks of a living-donor transplant.
items.explanation: **FSGS** recurs early and often in the graft.

items.stem: Eight years after transplant, a 41-year-old man on long-term immunosuppression develops fevers, night sweats and widespread lymph node enlargement. EBV DNA is detectable in the blood.
items.explanation: EBV-driven lymphoid proliferation in a transplant recipient = **PTLD**.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man without diabetes has IgA nephropathy, eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73 m² and ACR 85 mg/mmol despite a maximum dose of ramipril. BP is 128/78 mmHg and potassium 4.6 mmol/L.
questions.leadIn: Which additional drug class is best supported to slow his progression?
questions.explanation: **SGLT2 inhibitors** reduce the risk of progression by about 30–40% in proteinuric CKD **with or without diabetes** (eGFR above about 25). Dual RAAS blockade is avoided.
whyNot: Adding an ARB to an ACEi gives no renal benefit and more hyperkalaemia and AKI.
Combining a renin inhibitor with an ACEi is avoided for the same reason.
NSAIDs are nephrotoxic and should be avoided in CKD.
Raises potassium dangerously alongside an ACE inhibitor.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely answer from the list. Any option can be picked once, several times or not at all.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman with hypertension has eGFR 50 mL/min/1.73 m². Her mother started dialysis at 55. Ultrasound shows two large kidneys.
items.explanation: Inherited disease with **large kidneys** and a parent on dialysis = **ADPKD** (a reminder that big kidneys do not exclude CKD).

items.stem: A 72-year-old smoker with intermittent claudication and previous MI has slowly falling eGFR. Ultrasound shows one kidney 2 cm smaller than the other; urine is bland.
items.explanation: Asymmetric kidneys in a vasculopath suggest **atheromatous renovascular disease**.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man has had type 2 diabetes for 20 years. His ACR has risen steadily over the past 8 years and his eGFR is now 38 mL/min/1.73 m². There is no haematuria.
items.explanation: Long-standing diabetes with **progressive albuminuria** and bland sediment = **diabetic nephropathy**, the commonest cause of ESRD.

items.stem: A 38-year-old farmer grew up in a rural part of the Middle East where schistosomiasis is endemic. He has bilateral hydronephrosis with no stones and a normal prostate, and eGFR 35 mL/min/1.73 m².
items.explanation: Two steps: hydronephrosis without stones or prostatic disease = obstruction of another cause; a background in an endemic part of the Middle East = **schistosomiasis**.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the main indication for dialysis from the list, or that none is present. Any option can be picked once, several times or not at all.
options: Symptomatic uraemia impairing quality of life

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman on long-term lithium for bipolar disorder has vomiting, coarse tremor and confusion after a dehydrating illness. Her lithium level is markedly raised and creatinine has doubled.
items.explanation: Lithium is a **dialysable toxin** (the "I" of AEIOU).

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with CKD G5 (eGFR 9) has had months of poor appetite, nausea, itching, weight loss and fatigue that stop him gardening. K⁺ 5.4 mmol/L, bicarbonate 20 mmol/L, chest clear.
items.explanation: No emergency, but **uraemic symptoms** now impair his quality of life at eGFR about 10: the usual reason to start chronic dialysis.

items.stem: A 57-year-old woman with CKD G4 (eGFR 18, creatinine 340 µmol/L) feels well. K⁺ is 5.2 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, and she has no oedema.
items.explanation: Two steps: a lab number alone is not an indication, and she has no symptoms or refractory complications = **no current indication**. Plan access and preparation instead.

ospe.identify: Signs of advanced CKD: pallor, yellow tinge, scratch marks, bruising, brown-line nails, raised JVP, and RRT clues (fistula, dialysis line, Tenckhoff catheter, transplant scar).
Skin biopsy: calcified small arteries without vasculitis → calciphylaxis (calcific uraemic arteriolopathy).
CKD-MBD X-ray signs: subperiosteal erosions and pepperpot skull (hyperparathyroidism), rugger-jersey spine (osteosclerosis), Looser zones (osteomalacia).
Haemodialysis access: tunnelled cuffed catheter into the right atrium vs AV fistula (distended arterialised vein) vs AV graft.
IV cannula in the non-dominant forearm of a CKD patient → wrong site: these veins must be saved for a future fistula.
Left forearm radiocephalic AV fistula in a dialysis patient: flag it before surgery and never compress it, as it may thrombose.
Tenckhoff catheter for peritoneal dialysis, tip lying in the pelvis.
Transplant biopsy: endothelialitis (acute vascular rejection) vs glomerulitis with peritubular capillary C4d (antibody-mediated rejection).
